newsitem.title: USA: Hubble shows Texas-size dust storm on Mars.
newsitem.headline: Hubble shows Texas-size dust storm on Mars.

text.p: A Texas-size dust storm has been swirling around the Martian north pole for months, according to images released on Monday from the orbiting Hubble Space Telescope.

A salmon-coloured patch about 600 miles (965 km) across showed up in a picture of the Red Planet taken on Sept. 18. Scientists believe it is the first time one of Mars' huge storms has been located near the receding north polar ice cap.

By Oct. 15, the storm had broken up a bit, spreading into a comma-shaped streak across the cap, in a configuration similar to cold weather fronts on Earth, scientists at the Space Telescope Science Institute said in a statement.

They said the storm might have been caused by large temperature differences between the polar ice and warmer regions to the south, which are being heated by the Martian spring. Temperatures are not warm enough to melt the ice, however; instead, the ice sublimes -- goes from a solid to a gas -- and the polar cap shrinks.

The presence of water, even in the form of polar ice, is significant to the current inquiry into whether life might have existed on Mars. Since August, when the National Aeronautics and Space Administration unveiled a Martian meteorite found in Antarctica that showed evidence of what might be fossilized microscopic life from Mars, there has been global debate over whether such life is possible.
Last week, British astronomers said samples from two separate Martian meteorites showed definite traces that could have been left by living organisms.
Scientists hope to know more after two new missions to be launched this year start sending back data.

The Mars Global Surveyor, a NASA mission to launch on Wednesday, is expected to send back a new batch of pictures from high-resolution cameras. Another spacecraft will be launched in December carrying a robot-rover called Sojourner, which should arrive on Mars next July.
